title: Mazda and Chip Ganassi Racing Adopt OpenAI's Astra AI for Hardware Engineering
summary:
OpenAI has expanded the application of its GPT-6 Astra model to external engineering partners to automate physical design workflows. The company said Mazda's aerodynamics engineers use the AI to simulate nose shapes to reduce drag, while the American racing team Chip Ganassi Racing uses the tool to convert 3D scans of legacy parts into manufacturing drawings and editable CAD models. These industry deployments come as the use of AI engineering tools by OpenAI's own internal hardware teams has grown 23 fold since February.

The company recently demonstrated the model's capabilities through a project where two engineers used Astra to design a gadget for interacting with the Codex coding agent. Astra developed the electrical components, the printed circuit board layout, and the firmware for the device in less than a week, though OpenAI noted the AI still lacks a full understanding of factory tolerances and assembly details. These results follow the announcement of a newer unreleased internal model that achieved a 0.875 score on the BenchCAD 2.0 hardware design benchmark, surpassing GPT-6 Astra's peak score of 0.594.

selectedTweets.text:
Two engineers at OpenAI built a working device in under a week, as a side project, trying to make no direct human edits to the design.

OpenAI published the details yesterday. GPT-6 Astra, its newest model, wrote the functional requirements, designed the look and the enclosure, picked the electrical components, laid out the printed circuit board and wrote the firmware for a small gadget people use to talk to Codex, OpenAI's coding agent. A contract manufacturer built a first batch of prototypes in under a month. Getting it ready for production still took several rounds of review, because the model didn't always account for the factory's tolerances and assembly details. That is the next thing it will learn.

Inside OpenAI, model usage by the hardware teams has grown 23-fold since February. Mazda's aerodynamics engineers are using Astra to simulate dozens of nose shapes and find which features really cut drag. Chip Ganassi Racing, the American racing team, uses it to turn 3D scans of old parts into editable CAD models and manufacturing drawings.

At Fon we made our own Wi-Fi router, the Fonera. Hardware has always been slower and more expensive to improve than software, because every change means new parts and new prototypes.

Hardware is starting to move at the speed of software.
